meta.title: Zulu A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Zulu → English (see the Zulu, recall the meaning) and English → Zulu (see an English meaning, recall the Zulu). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Zulu, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 236 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, people and the family, numbers, time, the days of the week and the months, food and drink, money and shopping, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, animals, school and work, the everyday verbs, and the pronouns, question words and joining words every sentence is built out of — and the other 264 are the commonest remaining words of the Zulu Wikipedia, counted by the WHOLE word: Zulu joins its prefixes to the word (abantu, kumuntu, ngiyahamba), so every form of a noun or a verb is added together. That corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (history, government, sport). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and a few everyday words are missing from it (kodwa 'but', namuhla 'today', nini 'when'). A noun is shown whole with its NOUN CLASS — the prefix family that every adjective, verb and pronoun agreeing with it echoes; the Zulu Noun Classes deck, first in this collection, teaches them — and its plural and locative ('at, in, to'): 252 nouns here. A verb, an adjective or a relative is shown by its stem with a hyphen (-hamba, -khulu), as Zulu dictionaries print it, since none stands without a prefix; the 166 verbs give their infinitive and plural command, and behind the Tenses fold their present, negative, past and future by person, taken from Wiktionary's own tables. Beneath each headword is Wiktionary's tone-marked spelling (umúntu, -hámba): ordinary Zulu writing marks no tone, but the language has it. Example sentences are few: 57 of the 500 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about a hundred Zulu sentences; none is invented. A speaker reads the word and each sentence where the device has a Zulu voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes, forms, tables and tones: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Zulu Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
